section.title: The Twelve Sent Out
section.sectionRationale: The second of Matthew's five discourses is the Mission Discourse. Having felt compassion for the shepherdless crowds, Jesus now multiplies His ministry: He appoints twelve apostles, gives them His authority, and sends them to the lost sheep of Israel. His instructions move from the immediate mission to the long haul of persecution, fearless witness, and the costly, dividing allegiance He requires.
section.thesis: Jesus extends His own mission and authority through the twelve, sending them to proclaim the kingdom in radical dependence, and He prepares them for hatred and persecution with the promise of the Father's care and the Spirit's help, calling them to fearless confession and cross-bearing loyalty that treasures Him above life itself.
section.frameNote: Seven beats: the twelve named and empowered; sent to Israel with instructions; sheep among wolves facing persecution; the call to fear God alone under the Father's care; confessing or denying Christ; not peace but a sword and the cost of discipleship; and the reward of those who receive His messengers.

verses.text: And calling His twelve disciples to Him, Jesus gave them {{exousia|authority}} over unclean spirits, so that they could drive them out and heal every disease and sickness.
These are the names of the twelve {{apostolos|apostles}}: first Simon, called Peter, and his brother Andrew; James son of Zebedee, and his brother John;
Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus;
Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus.

units.label: Sent to the lost sheep
units.note: freely you have received, freely give

verses.text: These twelve Jesus sent out with the following instructions: “Do not go onto the road of the Gentiles or enter any town of the Samaritans.
Go rather to the lost sheep of Israel.
As you go, preach this message: ‘The kingdom of heaven is near.’
Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, drive out demons. Freely you have received; freely give.
Do not take along any gold or silver or copper in your belts.
Take no bag for the road, or second tunic, or sandals, or staff; for the worker is worthy of his provisions.
Whatever town or village you enter, find out who is worthy there and stay at his house until you move on.
As you enter the home, greet its occupants.
If the home is worthy, let your peace rest on it, but if it is not, let your peace return to you.
And if anyone will not welcome you or heed your words, shake the dust off your feet when you leave that home or town.
Truly I tell you, it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town.

units.label: Sheep among wolves
units.note: the Spirit of your Father will speak

verses.text: Behold, I am sending you out like sheep among wolves; therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves.
But beware of men, for they will hand you over to their councils and flog you in their synagogues.
On My account you will be brought before governors and kings as witnesses to them and to the Gentiles.
But when they hand you over, do not worry about how to respond or what to say. In that hour you will be given what to say.
For it will not be you speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.
Brother will betray brother to death, and a father his child; children will rise against their parents and have them put to death.
You will be hated by everyone because of My name, but the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.
When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next. Truly I tell you, you will not reach all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes.
A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a servant above his master.
It is enough for a disciple to be like his teacher, and a servant like his master. If the head of the house has been called Beelzebul, how much more the members of his household!

units.label: Fear God alone
units.note: the very hairs of your head are numbered

verses.text: So do not be afraid of them. For there is nothing concealed that will not be disclosed, and nothing hidden that will not be made known.
What I tell you in the dark, speak in the daylight; what is whispered in your ear, proclaim from the housetops.
Do not be afraid of those who kill the body but cannot kill the {{psyche|soul}}. Instead, fear the One who can destroy both soul and body in hell.
Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from the will of your Father.
And even the very hairs of your head are all numbered.
So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.
Therefore everyone who {{homologeo|confesses}} Me before men, I will also confess him before My Father in heaven.
But whoever denies Me before men, I will also deny him before My Father in heaven.

units.label: Not peace but a sword
units.note: take up your cross and follow

verses.text: Do not assume that I have come to bring peace to the earth; I have not come to bring peace, but a sword.
For I have come to turn ‘a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law.
A man’s enemies will be the members of his own household.’
Anyone who loves his father or mother more than Me is not worthy of Me; anyone who loves his son or daughter more than Me is not worthy of Me;
and anyone who does not take up his cross and follow Me is not worthy of Me.
Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for My sake will find it.
He who receives you receives Me, and he who receives Me receives the One who sent Me.
Whoever receives a prophet because he is a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward, and whoever receives a righteous man because he is a righteous man will receive a righteous man’s reward.
And if anyone gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones because he is My disciple, truly I tell you, he will never lose his reward.”

exousia.gloss: Authority, right, power. Jesus gives the twelve His own authority over unclean spirits and disease, so their ministry is an extension of His; they act not in their own power but as those sent and empowered by Him.

apostolos.gloss: Apostle, one sent with the sender's authority, an emissary or commissioned representative. The word appears here for the first time in Matthew, marking the twelve as Jesus' authorized envoys, sent to carry His message and mission.

psyche.gloss: Soul, life, the true self. Jesus contrasts the body, which men can kill, with the soul, which they cannot, urging His messengers to fear God rather than men and to lose their life for His sake in order to truly find it.

homologeo.gloss: To confess, acknowledge, openly own. To confess Christ before men is to publicly identify with Him whatever the cost; Jesus promises to acknowledge such a person before the Father, and warns that denial will be met with denial.

basic.context: Jesus appoints twelve apostles, gives them His authority over demons and disease, and sends them out. He tells them to go first to Israel with the message that the kingdom is near, to travel light in radical dependence, and to expect both welcome and rejection. Then He looks past this mission to the long future: persecution, family division, and hatred for His name, all met by the Father's care, the Spirit's help, and the promise of reward.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the discourse on two levels: the immediate mission of the twelve to Israel, and the wider, ongoing mission of the church that faces persecution. The instructions about no bag or staff belong to that first, urgent errand; the warnings about councils, governors, and Gentiles look further ahead. Throughout, the theme is fearless, costly witness under the Father's providence.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus gives the twelve His own authority and names them apostles, sent ones who carry His mission. He urges them to fear for the soul, the true self, more than the body, and to confess Him openly before men. To confess Christ publicly is to be owned by Him before the Father; to deny Him is to be denied.
basic.typology: The twelve apostles correspond to the twelve tribes, marking the reconstitution of God's people around Jesus. The messengers sent with Christ's authority continue the pattern of the prophets, hated and persecuted as they were. And the cross the disciples must take up points to the Master's own cross they are called to share.
basic.christ: Jesus is the sender who shares His authority and whose mission the apostles carry. He is worth more than father, mother, child, or life itself, a claim only God can make. He is present in His messengers, so that to receive them is to receive Him and the Father. And He is the Master whose sufferings His servants will share.
basic.god: The Father's providence rules the whole mission: not a sparrow falls apart from His will, and the hairs of our heads are numbered. He is the one to be feared above all who can kill the body, and the one who rewards even a cup of water given to a disciple. The Spirit of the Father speaks through persecuted witnesses.
basic.crossReferences: Micah 7:6 lies behind the family division Jesus foretells. Matthew 28 sends the disciples to all nations, completing what begins here with Israel. Acts 4 shows the apostles bearing witness before councils. And Luke 12 parallels the sayings about fearing God and confessing Christ.
basic.oneStory: The compassion that wept over the shepherdless crowds now becomes a mission. Jesus multiplies His ministry through the twelve, sending them first to Israel and then, in the church, to the nations, with a message of the kingdom and a warning of the cost. The King who gathers a people also sends them, promising His presence, the Father's care, and a reward that outlasts every loss.

context.literary:
Matthew gathers the teaching of Jesus into five great discourses, and each ends with a formula about Jesus having finished these sayings. This is the second. It is also the one that most clearly overlaps with its time frame, because it speaks in two registers at once. Verses 5 to 15 are bound to a single errand in Galilee: where to go, what to say, what to carry, whom to stay with. From verse 16 the horizon widens. Kings and governors, Gentiles, a brother betraying a brother, a hatred from everyone: these cannot have been met on a village circuit in a few weeks, and the discourse is plainly addressed past the twelve to every later messenger of Jesus. Matthew does not mark the shift with a new setting. The speech simply keeps going, which is how he wants the reader to hear it.

The passage opens with a list and closes with a promise, and each frames the other. The list of the twelve in verses 2 to 4 is the only place in the gospel where Matthew uses the word apostle, and the discourse then explains what that word means: sent ones who carry the authority of the one who sends them. At the end, verse 40 returns to the same idea, He who receives you receives Me, and the one who receives Me receives the One who sent Me. The chain runs Father, Son, apostle, host, and the discourse ends with the chain intact.

Within the main body the sayings are linked by three commands not to fear, in verses 26, 28 and 31, each followed by a reason: nothing will stay hidden, God can destroy soul and body, and you are worth more than many sparrows. Another thread is the word worthy, which turns up in the instructions about the household and the town and again in the demand for loyalty, in verses 10 to 13 and 37 to 38. The worthy worker and the worthy house prepare the reader for the sharper sense of being worthy of Jesus himself. The result is a speech that moves from practical advice to the stakes of allegiance without a seam.
context.historical:
The disciples are sent into the villages of Galilee, a region with a large Jewish population, a number of Gentile cities on its borders, and a strong tradition of itinerant teachers. Hospitality for a traveller was a sacred duty, and a household that took in a messenger took on something of his reputation. This is why the instruction to find out who is worthy matters. The first thing a visiting preacher did was to choose a home that would receive him and his message with credit.

The ban on gold, silver or copper, a bag, a second tunic, sandals and a staff has been read in different ways, and the different Gospels word it slightly differently. Mark 6:8 allows a staff and sandals, Matthew forbids both, and Luke 9:3 forbids the staff. The common point is plain: the messengers carry no reserve. They go as people whose supplies are a debt owed by the people they serve, which Jesus puts in the proverb of verse 10, the worker is worthy of his provisions, a principle Paul later applies to church workers, 1 Corinthians 9:14. Luke 22:35-36 records Jesus looking back at this trip and then changing the terms for a new situation.

Shaking the dust off the feet was a gesture with a history. Jews returning from Gentile lands were said to shake off the dust so as not to carry its impurity into the holy land, and to do the same to a Jewish town was to treat it as pagan. The comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah in verse 15, which Genesis 19:24-28 shows destroyed by fire, sets that gesture against the worst judgment story the audience knew.

The persecutions described were the experience of the first generation of the church. Synagogue floggings, appearances before councils, and the dragging of believers before governors and kings are all attested in Acts, for example Acts 5:40 and Acts 25 and 26. Family betrayal also had its sharpest edge in a culture where honour and obedience to family ran deep. Deuteronomy 13:6-9 had even told Israelites to hand over a brother or a child who led them to worship other gods, and the disciples, who were told to reject nothing but idolatry, would find themselves treated by their families as the idolaters. The name Beelzebul in verse 25 is the name that was already being thrown at Jesus in 9:34, and the household of verse 25 is His own.
context.canonical:
The twelve are numbered as a statement. Israel had twelve tribes, and when the nation was scattered, the prophets dreamed of a regathering of all twelve. By choosing exactly twelve, Jesus is acting out the claim that He is gathering and rebuilding Israel, and He says so directly in Matthew 19:28, when the Son of Man sits on His throne and they sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes. The picture closes the Bible: the gates of the new Jerusalem carry the names of the twelve tribes and its foundations the names of the twelve apostles, Revelation 21:12-14. The two groups of twelve are brought together in one city.

The restriction of verses 5 and 6, to the lost sheep of Israel, reflects the order of salvation history that the Bible keeps: the promise went first to Abraham's family and through it to the nations. The Canaanite woman in 15:24 hears the same limit, and Paul describes the same sequence, to the Jew first and then to the Greek, Romans 1:16. Within the same gospel the limit is lifted when the risen Lord says to make disciples of all nations, Matthew 28:19, and the discourse already glances ahead with its witness to the Gentiles in verse 18.

The sayings about persecution are taken up widely. Jesus repeats them in the Olivet discourse, Matthew 24:9-14, and Luke has parallels in 12:4-9 and 21:12-19. John records that the servant is not greater than his master, John 13:16 and 15:20, and Peter tells the scattered believers not to be surprised at the fiery trial, but to rejoice in sharing the sufferings of Christ, 1 Peter 4:12-14. Acts shows the promise of verse 20 at work, as Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, speaks before the rulers in Acts 4:8-13. Moses was told something similar at the burning bush, I will help you as you speak, Exodus 4:12, and the echo suggests that those sent by God are given what He demands.

Verses 35 and 36 quote Micah 7:6, in which the prophet describes a society so broken that the household itself is the enemy. Jesus applies that moment of national collapse to the division caused by His own coming. The saying about finding and losing a life returns in Matthew 16:25 and John 12:25, and the call to take up a cross is repeated in Matthew 16:24, so that the first mention of the cross in this gospel is placed here, years before Jesus carries His own.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wants the church of his own day to hear itself in this discourse. He is writing for people who had already been dragged before synagogues and magistrates, who knew what it was to be hated for the name of Jesus, and who needed to know that none of it took Him by surprise. By placing the warning on the lips of Jesus before the first mission, Matthew shows that the suffering of the church is not a sign that the plan has failed. It was foretold, and the same Lord who foretold it promised the Spirit's words and the Father's care.

He also wants the apostles to be seen as authorised. The list opens with the gift of authority and is followed by a clear chain of sending. The reader who hears of the twelve is meant to treat their word as the word of Jesus, and to hear in their rejection the rejection of Jesus Himself, which is why the hospitable are so blessed and the hostile so gravely warned.

Above all, Matthew intends the discourse to confront every reader with the claim of Christ. The sayings at the heart of the speech, verses 32 to 39, are not instructions for a mission; they are demands on a person. Anyone who wanted to belong to the movement had to settle who came first, and the answer Matthew gives is the answer of Jesus: He does. The author has gathered these sayings so that no reader could mistake discipleship for a pleasant association.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
A good deal here is narrowly tied to one mission and one moment. The ban on bag and staff, the restriction to Israel, the greeting of the household and the shaking of dust describe how the twelve were to go out on that occasion. Jesus Himself reworked the terms when circumstances changed, Luke 22:35-36, and the apostles in Acts go to Gentiles, carry resources and organise collections. Treating the first instructions as a rule for every missionary mistakes a particular errand for a permanent law, though the underlying principle, that the messenger depends on God and may expect support from those he serves, still stands, 1 Corinthians 9:14.

A second layer is promise. The Spirit will speak, the Father numbers the hairs, and no kindness will lose its reward. These are not conditions to meet but facts to rest in. They invite trust rather than action, and they should not be read as a guarantee that believers will escape suffering; the same chapter promises that some will be put to death.

A third layer is abiding command and it carries to every disciple: fear God and not men, confess Christ openly, love Him above family, take up the cross and receive His messengers. These are given to the twelve and to all who follow Jesus. The passage does not tell believers to seek persecution, and it explicitly allows flight in verse 23. It does not authorise violence, since the sword of verse 34 is a figure for division. And it does not teach that a household should be abandoned; it teaches that no household may take the place of Christ.

debates.question: What does Jesus mean by I have not come to bring peace, but a sword?

views.label: The gospel inevitably divides
views.case: Allegiance to Christ splits even families, as Micah 7:6 foretold; Jesus is not endorsing violence but describing the division His claims provoke between those who follow Him and those who reject Him.

views.label: A call to costly, undivided loyalty
views.case: The saying leads directly into loving Christ above family and taking up the cross; the sword names the painful cost of putting Jesus first, which severs lesser ties when they compete with Him.

debates.bearing: Both agree Jesus brings not the false peace of compromise but a division born of supreme allegiance to Him, though His ultimate aim is true peace with God.

debates.question: What does verse 23 mean, that they will not finish the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes?

views.label: A coming in judgment on that generation
views.case: Many read the coming of the Son of Man as His vindication and judgment, realized in events like the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, so the mission to Israel continues until that decisive coming.

views.label: The urgency and continuance of the mission until the end
views.case: Others take it that the task of witnessing to Israel will not be complete before Christ's final coming, stressing the ongoing urgency of mission until He returns in glory.

debates.bearing: Both hold that Jesus assures His messengers their mission has a divinely set horizon and that the Son of Man will surely come; the persecuted are to persevere until then.

debates.question: Why were the twelve forbidden to go to Gentiles and Samaritans, when the gospel is for all nations?

views.label: A matter of order, not exclusion
views.case: Israel was the people of promise, and the Messiah had to be offered to them first. Jesus makes the same point of Himself in 15:24, and Paul keeps the order in Romans 1:16. The limit is temporary and is lifted in 28:19.

views.label: A pointed message to Israel's leaders
views.case: The mission to the lost sheep sets Israel's failed shepherds against the true one, so that Israel is first called to account. The Gentile mission, by contrast, is already anticipated in the witness to Gentiles in verse 18, and the limit is a stage rather than a barrier.

debates.bearing: Both views hold that the restriction belongs to a stage in the story and not to the character of God, whose promise to Abraham always included the nations, and both see Matthew 28:19 as the point at which the stage ends.

study.originalLanguages:
The most repeated word in the discourse is axios, worthy. The worker is worthy of his provisions in verse 10, the household may be worthy or not in verses 11 and 13, and then Jesus says three times that the one who loves father or mother more than Him, or son or daughter more than Him, or who does not take up his cross, is not worthy of Him in verses 37 and 38. The word carries the sense of matching or balancing the scales. A messenger is worth his keep; a household shows its worth by how it responds to the message; and the disciple's whole life must weigh in on the side of Jesus. The same adjective rolls from payment to character to allegiance.

In verse 16 Jesus asks the disciples to be phronimoi like snakes and akeraioi like doves. Phronimos means wise in a practical, discerning way, and is the word used of the wise builder in Matthew 7:24. It is the word the Septuagint uses to describe the serpent's cunning in Genesis 3:1, so the saying quietly redeems a trait of the serpent into a virtue of the disciple. Akeraios means unmixed, without alloy, and Paul uses it of being innocent about what is evil, Romans 16:19. The pairing expects a wisdom that sees danger clearly and a purity that never uses the danger as an excuse for deceit.

Verse 22 promises that the one who hypomeno, remains under, to the end will be saved. The verb joins hypo, under, and meno, remain, and the picture is of staying beneath a weight without leaving. The same verb appears in the parallel in Matthew 24:13. It is the endurance of someone who has been loaded and does not set the load down.

In verses 28 and 39 the same noun appears in two English dress: psyche, translated soul in verse 28 and life in verse 39. English splits the word, but the Greek reader hears one word. Those who kill the body cannot kill the psyche, and the one who finds his psyche will lose it. The saying is a single idea about the self as God sees it. Verse 28 also names the place of destruction as geenna, the Greek form of the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a name Jesus uses elsewhere for final judgment, as in Matthew 5:29 and 23:33.

The verb for confess in verses 32 and 33 is homologeo, built from homo, same, and lego, say. To confess is to say the same thing, to agree with. Jesus then uses the same verb of Himself, I will confess him before My Father, so that the disciple's confession of Jesus before men is matched by Jesus' confession of the disciple before God. The echo is a covenant of mutual acknowledgment. Paul puts it in terms of the creed in Romans 10:9-10, where confessing Jesus as Lord is joined with belief in the heart. The opposite verb, arneomai, to deny or refuse to acknowledge, is the word used for Peter's later denial in Matthew 26:70.

Finally, the first appearance in Matthew of stauros, cross, is in verse 38. The disciples have not yet seen a cross, and the saying would have sounded to a Galilean audience like a reference to a Roman execution, the condemned man carrying the crossbeam to the place of death. The image is spoken to the twelve before any explanation, and it stands as a prediction of what the master Himself will carry.

typology.type: The twelve apostles and the twelve tribes
typology.fulfillment: The tribes were descended from Jacob's twelve sons, and when Israel was divided and exiled, the prophets looked for a restoration of the whole. Jesus names twelve men who stand for a renewed people, and in Matthew 19:28 He says they will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes. Revelation 21:12-14 carries the picture to its end, with the names of the tribes on the gates and the names of the apostles on the foundations. The pattern is of continuity, not replacement: the new people is built on the old. It falls short in that the twelve were mortal and one of them, Judas, fell, so that the number had to be restored in Acts 1:21-26. The sure foundation is the one on which they themselves stand.

The picture of the sheep in danger belongs to the long story of Israel's shepherds. In Matthew 9:36 the crowds are sheep without a shepherd; now the shepherd sends out His own sheep and tells them that wolves are waiting. Isaiah 53:7 describes the Servant as a lamb led to the slaughter who does not open His mouth, and the disciples are sent to follow that same road. The escalation is that the sheep are not left alone: the Shepherd goes before them, and in John 10:11 He lays down His life for them. The type falls short in that the Shepherd is also the Lamb, and His sufferings are the ones that save, while theirs are a witness and a sharing, not an atonement, Colossians 1:24.

typology.type: The messenger who bears the sender's authority
typology.fulfillment: A messenger in the ancient world stood in the place of the one who sent him, and the Old Testament prophets spoke with a formula, thus says the LORD. Jesus extends the pattern: the apostles carry His word as He carries the Father's, so that to receive them is to receive Him and the One who sent Him, as John 13:20 and Luke 10:16 also say. The pattern is complete in the Son Himself, who is the final Word from God, Hebrews 1:1-2. It falls short because the apostles speak with delegated authority only, and their message is always the message of the one who sent them, not their own, 2 Corinthians 4:5.

typology.type: The cross as the road of the disciple
typology.fulfillment: The cross of verse 38 is the first mention in the gospel, and it is a picture of the road that the Master Himself will go. Matthew 16:24 repeats the call after Jesus first predicts His death, and Luke 14:27 adds that no one can be a disciple who does not carry his own cross and follow. The correspondence is that the disciple takes the same road as the teacher, and the escalation is that the Master actually dies on the cross while the disciple carries it in a life of self-denial. The type is not complete in us: He alone carried the weight of sin there, 1 Peter 2:24, and we follow Him as those who have been carried.

study.christ:
This discourse leads to Christ more by the claims He makes than by a single prophecy, and the claims are staggering. He gives the twelve His own authority, the same authority He has displayed in chapters 8 and 9 over spirits and disease, and He gives it with a word. No prophet of the Old Testament delegated his own power; each spoke in the name of the LORD. Jesus speaks and acts in His own name, and the apostles carry His name into the world. Acts shows what that means, for in Acts 4:12 Peter says salvation exists in no one else, and the name is the name of Jesus.

The chain of sending in verse 40 places Jesus in the middle of a line that runs from the Father to the Father's messenger. To receive the twelve is to receive Him, and to receive Him is to receive the One who sent Him. This is a claim to be the face of God to the world: the way a person treats Jesus is the way he treats the Father. Jesus will say the same of the least of His brothers in Matthew 25:40, and the Gospel of John records that whoever receives the one He sends receives Him, John 13:20.

Even more startling are the demands in verses 37 to 39. In the Law, love of God is to rule over the whole heart, and a command to love someone more than family would be a command to idolatry. Moses had even praised the Levites for setting aside family when the covenant was at stake, Deuteronomy 33:9. Jesus asks the disciple to put Him before father, mother, son and daughter, and to be ready to lose his life for His sake. Only God can rightly ask this, and Jesus asks it of Himself. Luke 14:26 states the demand in the language of hating by comparison, so the point is clear: no other loyalty may rival Him.

The coming of the Son of Man in verse 23 recalls Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man is given dominion over all peoples forever. The same figure who is now sending lambs among wolves will be seen to hold the kingdom. The persecuted can be sure that their Lord is not defeated; His authority is the authority of the Son of Man in Daniel.

He is also the one who goes first. The household of verse 25 has been called Beelzebul, and the head of the house is Jesus. The servant who suffers like his master is a servant who shares the road of the Master, and the Master's road leads through a cross, which He mentions here before He tells the twelve in detail that it is coming. The offering of life in verse 39 is what Jesus will do first and best, Mark 10:45. He is the one who lost His life for the sake of the Father and found it on the third day.

A caution applies. The discourse is not a coded foretelling of the cross in every detail, and the sparrows, the dust and the cup of water are not riddles. The links above rest on what Jesus says here about Himself and on how the New Testament writers draw out the same claims.
study.god:
The God of this discourse is a Father, and the title is repeated in nearly every unit. The Spirit of your Father speaks in verse 20, the will of your Father governs the sparrow in verse 29, and the Father in heaven stands before the confessor and the denier in verses 32 and 33. The title is not sentimental. It is bound to authority and care in a single picture, the God who holds all things and who attends to the smallest of them.

His care is shown by two small images. Sparrows were the cheapest thing sold for food, and not one falls apart from the will of the Father. The hairs of the head are numbered. The images do not promise that the disciples will not be killed, because the discourse has just said that some will be. They tell the disciples that no death happens outside His knowledge and that nothing about them is overlooked. The logic of verse 31 is an argument from the lesser to the greater: if God notices the sparrow, how much more His own people. The parallel in Luke 12:6 adds that not one of them is forgotten by God, and Luke 21:18 says that not a hair of their heads will perish, a statement that stands alongside the prediction of death and is understood of final safety.

He is also the one who must be feared. Verse 28 is not a contradiction of His fatherly care but its necessary partner. A God who numbers hairs is a God who can destroy both soul and body, and the proper fear of Him is what frees His people from every other fear. Verses 26 to 31 hold the two truths together: the fear of God removes the fear of man, and the care of God removes the terror from the fear of God. Neither is allowed to cancel the other.

He is a God who speaks through His people. The promise of verse 20 is that the Spirit of the Father will speak through the persecuted, an echo of Exodus 4:12, where the LORD says to Moses, I will help you as you speak. The doctrine of the Spirit here is practical: the Spirit is the one who supplies the right words at the right moment, and Acts shows it at work in the speech of Peter in Acts 4:8.

He is a God who rewards and does not forget. The prophet's reward, the righteous man's reward and the reward for a cup of cold water are all promised in verses 41 and 42, and Hebrews 6:10 states the principle: God is not unjust and will not forget the work and love shown for His name. The reward is not a bargain; it is the Father's recognition of what is done for His Son.

For worship, the discourse teaches that the right posture before God is a mixture of awe and trust that is easily lost when only one half is remembered. Believers who know only His majesty are afraid of Him, and believers who know only His kindness forget to take Him seriously. Here they learn to speak openly about Christ because they are known by the Father, and to endure because the Father sees.

crossReferences.note: Jesus promises the twelve that they will sit on twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel when the Son of Man sits on His glorious throne. It explains why exactly twelve are named in Matthew 10 and sets the apostles' present hardships against their future place in the renewal of all things.

The gates of the new Jerusalem carry the names of the twelve tribes and the foundations carry the names of the twelve apostles. The two groups that Jesus brings together in His choice of the twelve are joined in the final city.

Mark tells of the same sending, but the twelve go out two by two and may take a staff and sandals. Reading it alongside Matthew shows that the point of the instructions is a lack of reserve and not a fixed list, and it warns against building a rule on a single detail.

Jesus asks the disciples whether they lacked anything when He sent them without purse or bag, and then reverses the instruction for the hours ahead. It shows that the rules of Matthew 10:9-10 belonged to a particular mission and that the Lord Himself adjusted them.

The sending of the seventy repeats much of the same advice, with lambs among wolves, peace on the house, and the dust wiped off the feet, and it compares an unreceptive town with Sodom. The overlap shows that Jesus taught these instructions more than once as a standing pattern of mission.

Moses says he is slow of speech, and the LORD answers that He made the mouth and will help him speak and teach him what to say. It is the root of the promise in verses 19 and 20, that the Spirit of the Father will give the persecuted witness what to say.

The prophet describes a corrupt age in which a son dishonours his father and a man's enemies are in his own house. Jesus draws on the verse in verses 35 and 36 to say that His coming will lay bare divisions even inside families.

The one like a son of man is given dominion over all peoples and an everlasting kingdom. Matthew 10:23 speaks of the coming of the Son of Man, and Daniel's vision gives the title its weight: the one who sends lambs among wolves holds the final authority.

Luke records the sayings about fearing God rather than those who kill the body, the sparrows, the numbered hairs and the confession before men. Placing the two versions side by side shows that these sayings were part of the general teaching of Jesus and not only of the mission discourse.

Jesus repeats the call to take up the cross and the saying about finding and losing a life, now in a scene where He first speaks plainly about His own death. The earlier statement in 10:38 prepares for it, and the later one shows the cost to which the earlier points.

The servant is not greater than his master, and whoever receives the one Jesus sends receives Him and the One who sent Him. John gives the same two sayings that Matthew places at the end of this discourse, which shows how deeply they were remembered.

Peter tells believers not to be surprised at the fiery trial, as if something strange were happening, but to rejoice at sharing the sufferings of Christ. It is a late echo of the promise and warning of Matthew 10:22 to 25, and it shows how fully the church absorbed the teaching.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story is the story of a God who sends. He sent Adam to tend the garden and Abraham to a land He would show him. He sent Moses to Pharaoh and the prophets to Israel, and when they would not listen He sent His Son, Matthew 21:37. Matthew 10 is the moment when the Son in turn sends others, and the structure of the Bible's story changes: for the first time, the messenger of God hands his commission to a company of ordinary men, and the sending is shared.

The passage answers questions that run back to the beginning. The promise of Genesis 12:3 was that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham, and the twelve are the beginning of that blessing's long arc. The scattered tribes of Israel are called again to be one people around the Messiah, as the prophets said, and the choice of twelve is a sign of it. The lost sheep of Israel were the ones Ezekiel said had no shepherd, and the Shepherd now sends out the first undershepherds. The wolves are the old enemies of the sheep, and the hatred the twelve will meet is the hatred the prophets met before them.

It sets up what comes next. Matthew's gospel moves at once into the rejection of chapters 11 and 12 and then to the parables of the kingdom, so that the warnings given here are borne out in the story that follows. The mission to Israel is limited in time, and it is widened in the closing words of the gospel, where the authority the risen Lord holds in heaven and on earth is the authority He earlier gave them, now for all nations, Matthew 28:18-20. The book of Acts opens with the apostles as witnesses to the ends of the earth, Acts 1:8, and its pages are the record of verses 17 to 20 coming true.

The end of the story is also in view. The Son of Man will come, and the apostles will sit on thrones. The one who confessed Christ before men will be confessed by Christ before the Father, and the cup of cold water will not lose its reward. In the new creation the names of the twelve are written on the foundations of the city, Revelation 21:14, and the people who were hated by everyone will be seen to belong to Him. The old promise that the sheep would not be left without a shepherd ends in the vision of Revelation 7:17, where the Lamb shepherds the multitude and God wipes away every tear.

quiz.q: What did Jesus give the twelve, and where did He first send them?

options.text: His authority over demons and disease, and He sent them to the lost sheep of Israel.
options.note: Verses 1 and 6 give both the authority and the initial mission field.

options.text: His authority, and He sent them at once to all the Gentile nations.
options.note: The worldwide mission comes later; here they are sent first to Israel, not the Gentiles.

options.text: A new law to teach, and He sent them to Jerusalem.
options.note: He gave them authority and a kingdom message, and sent them to Israel's towns, not specifically to Jerusalem with a new law.

options.text: Money and provisions, and He sent them to the Samaritans.
options.note: He told them to take no money and not to enter Samaritan towns on this mission.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus tell the disciples not to fear those who persecute them?

options.text: Because they can kill the body but not the soul, and the Father who numbers their hairs cares for them.
options.note: Verses 28-31 ground fearlessness in fearing God and trusting the Father's care.

options.text: Because persecution will never actually reach them.
options.note: Jesus plainly warns persecution will come; the comfort is God's care, not immunity from suffering.

options.text: Because the authorities have no real power to harm them.
options.note: The authorities can kill the body; the point is that God guards the soul and rewards faithfulness.

options.text: Because they should fear no one and nothing at all.
options.note: Jesus tells them to fear God, the One who holds soul and body, even as they do not fear men.

quiz.q: What does Jesus promise about confessing Him before others?

options.text: He will confess before the Father those who confess Him, and deny those who deny Him.
options.note: Verses 32-33 state both the promise and the warning.

options.text: He will reward public confession with earthly success.
options.note: The promise is acknowledgment before the Father, not earthly success.

options.text: Confession is a private matter that need not be spoken.
options.note: Jesus specifically speaks of confessing Him before men, a public acknowledgment.

options.text: Everyone will be accepted regardless of whether they confess Him.
options.note: Jesus warns that denial before men meets denial before the Father.

quiz.q: What does Jesus mean that He came not to bring peace but a sword?

options.text: Allegiance to Him inevitably divides, even families, as loyalty to Christ comes first.
options.note: Verses 34-37 describe the division His claims provoke and the priority He demands.

options.text: He calls His followers to take up literal weapons.
options.note: The sword is the division caused by the gospel, not a call to violence; this misreads the image.

options.text: He opposes peace of any kind between people.
options.note: He brings true peace with God; the division is the cost of undivided loyalty, not opposition to all peace.

options.text: He came only to start conflict for its own sake.
options.note: The division flows from supreme allegiance to Him, not conflict for its own sake.

quiz.q: What does Jesus say about those who receive His messengers?

options.text: To receive them is to receive Him and the One who sent Him, and even a cup of water is rewarded.
options.note: Verses 40-42 identify Jesus with His messengers and promise reward for kindness to them.

options.text: Only receiving prophets, not ordinary disciples, brings any reward.
options.note: Even a cup of water to a lowly disciple is rewarded, not only welcoming prophets.

options.text: Hospitality to the messengers earns nothing in particular.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus promises such kindness will never lose its reward.

options.text: The messengers must never accept anyone's hospitality.
options.note: Jesus assumes they will be received and stay in worthy homes.

questions: Jesus sent ordinary men, including a tax collector and a zealot, as His authorized messengers. How does it encourage you that God sends flawed people to carry His mission?
The disciples were to travel light, depending on God's provision. Where is God calling you to greater dependence on Him rather than on your own resources?
Jesus said to fear the One who holds the soul rather than those who can only harm the body. How would a right fear of God reorder the lesser fears that control you?
Jesus asks to be loved more than family and treasured above life itself. Is there a relationship or comfort you are tempted to put ahead of Him, and what would it look like to put Him first?
Whoever loses his life for Christ's sake will find it. Where is Jesus inviting you to lose something for His sake, trusting that you will gain far more in Him?

translationNotes.note: Cleanse the lepers refers to those afflicted with skin disease under Leviticus 13; the disciples are given Jesus' own healing authority to extend His ministry.
Take no staff on this specific mission; Jesus later adjusts such instructions for a different time, Luke 22:35-36, showing these were situational, not permanent rules.
The words about family division quote Micah 7:6, describing the household strife that allegiance to Christ can provoke.
